en: The Record of the Dharma-Abiding as Spoken by the Great Arhat Nandimitra,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus it is heard:
eight hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the Blessed One,
King Jayavarman ruled over the capital of Siṃhala Island.
There was an arhat named Nandimitra (translated into Chinese as Qingyou), who possessed the eight liberations,
the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of aspiration, the concentration of the ultimate limit, and so forth.
He is fully endowed with immeasurable merit.
Possessing great majestic power and a far-reaching reputation,
he is able, through the power of his vows and wisdom, to know the various mental activities of all sentient beings in this realm.
Furthermore, he was able to act in accordance with their needs to bring them various benefits.
When his work of transformation was complete and he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he gathered the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others.
He speaks of the various sublime qualities realized by himself,
as well as the excellent deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings that ought to be performed, all of which have been fully accomplished.
He addressed the assembly, saying:
"From this day forward, there is nothing further to be done;
only the state of nirvana without remainder is the goal to which we shall resort."
"Virtuous ones, you should know that there are matters of doubt for which you may ask questions.
When the great assembly heard these words,
they raised their voices in lamentation, unable to restrain themselves, and rolled upon the ground.
Some may raise their voices and declare: "The Buddha, the Bhagavān, has long since entered parinirvāṇa;
his noble disciples have likewise followed him into extinction.
The world has long been empty, devoid of a true Tamer."
Now you alone, Venerable Sir, are the eye of gods and humans.
How can you wish to abandon us? We pray that you will show compassion and grant us the gift of your remaining life for a short while longer.
The Venerable Śākyamitra consoled the assembly, saying:
"There is no need to weep.
You should know, sirs, that it is the natural law of the world that whatever is born must necessarily perish."
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, having subdued the four māras and attained mastery over their lifespan,
nevertheless manifest parinirvāṇa in accordance with worldly conventions;
how much more so should I, now, not remain forever?
Even if I were to grant your request, it would bring no benefit.
You should understand this meaning and not give rise to distress.
However, if you have any doubts, you should ask about them immediately.
Although the bhikṣus had received this instruction,
they remained choked with tears for a long while before finally asking:
"We do not yet know, World-Honored One Śākyamuni, how long the Unsurpassed True Dharma shall remain."
The Venerable One said:
"Listen attentively.
The Tathāgata has already previously taught the *Dharmasthitī-sūtra*."
I shall now briefly explain this further for you:
when the Buddha, the Bhagavān, was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the unsurpassed Dharma to sixteen great arhats and their retinues.
He causes them to protect and uphold [the Dharma] so that it does not perish or disappear;
furthermore, he commands their bodies to serve as true fields of merit for all donors,
enabling those who give to obtain great rewards.
When the great assembly had heard these words, their grief and sorrow were somewhat alleviated.
They requested again, saying:
"Regarding the sixteen Great Arhats you have mentioned..."
"We do not know what their names are.
Kalyāṇamitra replied,
"The name of the first elder is Piṇḍola-bharadvāja."
The second elder was named Kāṇakavatsa; the third elder was named Kāṇakavarmī;
the fourth elder was named Subhadra.
The fifth venerable one was named Nakula;
the sixth venerable one was named Bhadra;
the seventh venerable one was named Kālika.
The eighth venerable one was named Vatsīputra;
the ninth venerable one was named Śobhita;
the tenth venerable one was named Panthaka.
The eleventh elder was named Rāhula;
the twelfth elder was named Nāgasena; the thirteenth elder was named Upagupta.
The fourteenth venerable one was named Vanavāsin.
The fifteenth venerable one was named Aśvita.
The sixteenth venerable one was named Cūdapanthaka.
These sixteen great arhats were all endowed with immeasurable merits,
such as the three knowledges (*traividya*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
Free from the defilements of the triple world, they recited and upheld the Tripiṭaka and were extensively learned in non-Buddhist scriptures.
In accordance with the Buddha’s command,
I shall employ my supernormal powers to extend my own lifespan,
remaining to constantly protect and uphold the World-Honored One’s True Dharma for as long as it is destined to abide.
Furthermore, they act as true fields of merit for their donors,
enabling those who give to obtain great rewards.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others...
They requested once more, saying,
"We do not know where the sixteen venerable ones mostly dwell as they protect and uphold the True Dharma and benefit sentient beings."
Kalyāṇamitra replied,
"The foremost elder, together with his own retinue of one thousand arhats,
resides for the most part on the continent of Aparagoyānī."
The second Elder, together with his own retinue of five hundred arhats,
mostly resided in the northern kingdom of Kaśmīra.
The third Elder, together with his own retinue of six hundred arhats, [resided likewise].
For the most part, he resides on the continent of Pūrvavideha.
The fourth elder, together with his own retinue of seven hundred arhats,
for the most part resides on the continent of Uttarakuru.
The fifth Elder, together with his own retinue of eight hundred arhats,
mostly resides on Jambudvīpa in the south. The sixth Elder,
together with his own retinue of nine hundred arhats, [mostly resides on Jambudvīpa in the south].
For the most part, they dwell on the continent of Tamradvīpa.
The seventh Elder, together with his retinue of one thousand arhats,
dwells for the most part on the continent of Saṃghāṭa.
The eighth elder, together with his own retinue of one thousand one hundred arhats,
mostly resides on the continent of Pūrnadvīpa. The ninth elder,
together with his own retinue of nine hundred arhats, [mostly resides on the continent of Śāthadvīpa].
For the most part, he dwells on Mount Gandhamādana.
The tenth elder, together with his own retinue of one thousand three hundred arhats,
for the most part dwells in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The eleventh elder, together with his own retinue of one thousand one hundred arhats,
resides for the most part on the continent of Pūrvavideha. The twelfth elder,
together with his own retinue of one thousand two hundred arhats, [resides on the continent of Aparagoyānī].
For the most part, he dwells on Mount Mandāra.
The thirteenth elder, together with his retinue of one thousand three hundred arhats,
for the most part dwells on Mount Vipula.
The fourteenth elder, together with his own retinue of one thousand four hundred arhats,
mostly dwells on Mount Kṣemaka. The fifteenth elder,
together with his own retinue of one thousand five hundred arhats, [dwells there].
For the most part, he dwells on Vulture Peak Mountain.
The sixteenth elder, together with his retinue of one thousand six hundred arhats,
for the most part dwells on Mount Yugaṃdhara.
O virtuous ones, if in this world all kings,
ministers, great officials, elders, and householders—
whether men or women— should give rise to a profound and pure mind.
One may establish a great assembly for almsgiving for the Saṃgha of the four directions;
or establish a five-year unobstructed (pañcavārṣika) assembly;
or establish a great assembly to celebrate a temple, an image, a scripture, a banner, or the like.
Alternatively, they may invite monks to their own residence to establish a great assembly for merit;
or they may go to places such as the walking paths within a monastery and arrange superior and exquisite seats and bedding.
They offered robes, medicine, food, and drink to the assembly of monks;
at that time, these sixteen great arhats and their retinues dispersed and proceeded to their respective locations as was appropriate for each.
Manifesting in various forms, they concealed their noble demeanor and mingled with ordinary people,
secretly accepting offerings so that all donors might obtain supreme karmic rewards.
Thus, these sixteen great arhats,
who protect and uphold the true Dharma and benefit sentient beings,
have arrived here in Jambudvīpa at a time when the human lifespan has become extremely short, reaching only ten years.
When the kalpa of weapons arises and people slaughter one another,
the Buddha-dharma shall temporarily perish. Following the kalpa of weapons,
the lifespan of humans will gradually increase until it reaches the stage of one hundred years.
When the people of this continent grew weary of the suffering and harm caused by the previous calamity of weapons and took pleasure again in cultivating wholesome deeds,
those sixteen great arhats, together with their retinues,
returned once more among human beings.
He proclaimed and expounded the unsurpassed True Dharma,
leading immeasurable multitudes to leave the household life and performing acts of benefit for all sentient beings.
In this manner, it continues until the time when the human lifespan in this continent reaches sixty thousand years;
at that time, the unsurpassed True Dharma circulates in the world, blazing forth without ceasing.
Later, when the human lifespan reaches seventy thousand years, [the True Dharma will likewise flourish].
When the unsurpassed True Dharma was on the verge of being forever extinguished and vanished, these sixteen great Arhats,
together with their retinues, assembled here upon the land of this continent.
By means of his supernormal powers, he constructed a stūpa out of various seven treasures,
magnificent, high, and vast, within which were gathered all the bodily relics of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni.
At that time, the sixteen great arhats,
together with their retinues, circumambulated the stūpa, making offerings of various fragrant flowers while paying homage and offering praise.
Having circumambulated it a hundred thousand times and gazed upon it with reverence,
they all ascended into the air toward the stūpa and spoke these words:
"We pay homage to the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Having received these instructions, I have protected and upheld the True Dharma and brought benefit to devas and humans.
Now that the treasury of the Dharma has been exhausted and those with whom I had affinity have all been reached, I now bid farewell and enter parinirvāṇa.
Having spoken these words, they simultaneously entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Through the power of their prior vows and meditative concentration, fire arose and consumed their bodies;
like the extinguishing of a lamp's flame, not even a trace of bone remained.
At that moment, the stūpa sank into the earth and came to rest only upon reaching the level of the golden wheel.
At that time, the unsurpassed True Dharma of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni—
In this trichiliocosm, they were forever extinguished and no longer appeared;
from that time on, there was no further news of them. Yet, within this buddha-field, seventy billion pratyekabuddhas simultaneously appeared.
When the lifespan of the Tathāgata reaches eighty thousand years,
the assembly of Pratyekabuddha Āryas will likewise all pass into parinirvāṇa.
Subsequently, when Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, Jambudvīpa will be vast, magnificent, and pure, free from all thorns, ravines, valleys, mounds, and hillocks.
The ground is level, smooth, and moist, covered with golden sand.
Everywhere there are clear ponds, lush forests, famous flowers, auspicious grasses, and clusters of various jewels,
all reflecting one another in a manner most delightful to behold.
All people cultivate a compassionate heart and practice the ten wholesome deeds.
Because they cultivate goodness, their lifespans are long and they enjoy abundance, happiness, and tranquility.
Men and women are so numerous that the cities and towns stand close together, such that a rooster’s flight reaches from one to the next.
The crops cultivated there yield seven harvests from a single sowing;
they ripen naturally without the need for weeding or tilling.
O virtuous ones, during that time—
The adornments of the realm and the karmic fruits for sentient beings are too vast to be fully described,
as set forth in detail in the *Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*.
Once the Tathāgata Maitreya has attained perfect enlightenment, [the following shall occur].
For the sake of the assembly of śrāvakas, he preached the Dharma in three assemblies to cause them to transcend birth and death and attain realization of nirvāṇa.
In the first assembly, he delivered ninety-six koṭis of śrāvakas.
In the second assembly, he delivered ninety-four koṭis of śrāvakas;
in the third assembly, he delivered ninety-two koṭis of śrāvakas.
As for all kings, ministers, elders, householders, men, women, and all patrons—
Now, within the True Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha,
one is able to perform the work of a Buddha by planting roots of goodness for oneself,
or by teaching others to plant them— namely, using the seven treasures: gold, silver, pearls, jade, precious incense wood, brass, copper, iron, wood, stone, clay, or lacquer.
Whether using silk thread or colored pigments,
one may fashion images of the Buddha and stūpas, whether large or small,
even down to the smallest size, such as the measure of a finger joint.
Or they may make offerings with incense, flowers,
and various exquisite ritual implements, whether many or few;
by the power of such roots of goodness, they [attain these results].
When Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, one will successfully obtain a human body;
within that Buddha’s first assembly, with pure faith, one will renounce worldly life, shave off hair and beard, don the dharma robes, and thus join the ranks of the noble assembly.
In accordance with the power of their past vows, they immediately attain nirvana.
This is called the first kind of karmic fruit obtained by those who have planted roots of goodness for the sake of the Buddha’s work.
As for all kings, ministers, commoners, and all patrons:
Now, within the True Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha,
they are able to perform acts of Dharma to plant their own roots of goodness,
or to teach others to plant them as well.
This refers to all Mahāyāna sūtras associated with profound emptiness within the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka,
such as the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
The Sūtra of the White Lotus of the Sublime Dharma,
the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra,
and the Vajrapāṇi-garbha Sūtra.
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra, the Māyopama Samādhi Sūtra,
and the Mahāvikurvāṇa Samādhi Sūtra.
The Samādhi Sūtra of Gathering All Meritorious Qualities;
the Samādhi Sūtra of Returning to the Seal of Tathāgata Wisdom;
the Samādhi Sūtra of Possessing All Majestic Splendor.
The Ratnavyūha-sūtra, the Sarvabodhisattvasamādhi-saṃgraha-sūtra,
the Sarvabuddhaparigraha-sūtra,
and the Paripṛcchā-saṃgraha-sūtra.
The Brahmā-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra, the Subhūti-paripṛcchā-sūtra,
the Śūraṅgama-paripṛcchā-sūtra,
and the Pūrṇa-paripṛcchā-sūtra.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Nāga King Sāgara;
the Sūtra of the Questions of the Nāga King Anavatapta;
and the Sūtra of the Questions of the Nāga King Druma-ketu.
The Ratnapāṇiparipṛcchā-sūtra,
the Ratnaśikhīparipṛcchā-sūtra,
and the Gaganasvaraparipṛcchā-sūtra.
The *Gaganagañjaparipṛcchā-sūtra*,
the *Māyājālaparipṛcchā-sūtra*,
and the *Ratnadharmavilāsāparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Wondrous Woman;
the Sūtra of the Questions of Subāhu;
the Sūtra of the Questions of Siṃha.
The *Sūtra of the Questions of Caṇḍa*,
the *Sūtra of the Questions of Suvarṇaprabhāsā*,
and the *Sūtra on the Exposition of Akṣayamati*.
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra,
the Ajātaśatru-kaukṛtyavinodana Sūtra,
and the Satyasiddhi Sūtra.
The Nārāyaṇa Sūtra,
the Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra,
and the Padmapāṇi Sūtra.
The Scripture on the Names of Ten Buddhas;
the various scriptures on Immeasurable Light;
and the various scriptures on Sukhāvatī.
The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*,
and the *Sarvabuddhadharmapraveśa-sūtra*.
The Ratnaketu Sūtra,
the Ratnarāśi Sūtra,
and the Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra.
The *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the *Uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra*,
and other such Mahāyāna sūtras.
There are one hundred koṭis of distinct schools and factions;
furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna Vinaya-piṭaka and numerous categories within the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
All of these are subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
Furthermore, there is the Śrāvaka Tripiṭaka,
namely the Sūtra Piṭaka.
The Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidharma Piṭaka,
and the Sūtra Piṭaka.
There are five Āgamas, namely: the Dīrgha-āgama,
the Madhyama-āgama, [the Saṃyukta-āgama,
the Ekottarika-āgama, and the Kṣudraka-āgama].
The Ekottarika Āgama, the Saṃyukta Āgama, and the Kṣudraka Āgama.
Within the Vinaya Piṭaka, there are the Bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra and the Bhikṣuṇī-śīla-sūtra,
as well as the Vibhaṅga, the Prakaraṇa-grantha, the Skandhaka-vibhāga,
and the Mahāvaibhaṣika-śāstra (Aṅguttara-nikāya). Within the Abhidharma Piṭaka—
There are numerous categories, such as the *Ṣaṭpraśnavyākaraṇa*, the *Prasthāna*, and so forth;
furthermore, there are the *Jātakamālā* and the *Pratyekabuddhamālā*.
Within such repositories of the true Dharma,
there are those spoken by the Buddha, those spoken by Bodhisattvas, those spoken by Śrāvakas, those spoken by various ṛṣis,
those spoken by devas, or those spoken by wise men.
One who is capable of bringing about meaningful benefit,
even to the extent of their ability, whether reciting these four-line verses themselves or teaching others to recite them.
Whether one reads it oneself or causes others to read it;
whether one upholds it oneself or causes others to uphold it;
whether one explains it oneself or causes others to explain it.
Or they may reverently make offerings to the Dharma Master,
or reverently make offerings to the scriptural volumes—
namely, by means of various kinds of incense, flowers, banners, canopies, music, and lamps.
Or they may adorn a scripture with various multicolored bags, cloths, and silk ribbons;
by the power of such roots of goodness,
when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect awakening, they will obtain a human body that is well-manifested.
In that Buddha’s second assembly,
he abandoned the household life with pure faith and went forth into homelessness.
Having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the dharma robes, they have joined the assembly of the noble ones;
by the power of their prior vows, they immediately attain nirvana.
This is called the second kind of fruition obtained by those who plant roots of goodness for the sake of the Dharma.
If various kings, ministers, commoners,
and all other donors, within the True Dharma of the present Śākyamuni Buddha,
are able to perform services for the Saṃgha and personally plant roots of goodness;
Or he instructs others to plant [seeds],
namely the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs,
whether by regular invitation or according to circumstances.
On the first day of the month, or the eighth day, or the fifteenth day, one should prepare a vegetarian feast as an offering;
or go to a monastery to make offerings to the Buddha,
or to the Saṃgha, or to serve them.
Some may make offerings to those who cultivate meditative concentration;
some may make offerings to those who preach the Dharma;
or they may see someone wishing to study and propagate the True Dharma.
One should listen to and receive instruction from the teacher without creating obstacles;
one should provide what is necessary for their comfort so as not to cause them to become timid or retreat.
Or, one may establish a five-year unrestricted almsgiving assembly (*pañcavārṣika-mahāpariṣad*).
Some give to the Saṃgha of the four directions;
some give to monasteries, as well as seats and bedding;
some give bells and chimes; or they give gardens and groves.
By making such offerings to the Saṅgha,
through the power of these roots of goodness,
they will obtain a human body when Maitreya Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment.
In the third assembly of that Buddha,
with pure faith he abandoned the household life to go forth into homelessness;
having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, he joined the ranks of the noble community.
In accordance with the power of his past vows, he immediately attained nirvāṇa.
This is called the third kind of fruit and retribution obtained by those who plant roots of goodness for the sake of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the great arhat Ānanda (Yìngyǒu) [spoke thus].
Having extensively explained the matters above for the great assembly,
he used his supernormal powers to rise into the air before the assembly to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
He manifested various kinds of inconceivable twin miracles (*yamaka-prātihārya*),
causing those who witnessed them to advance upon the supreme path.
When that Venerable One had thus displayed his miraculous powers,
He then sat cross-legged in mid-air,
relinquished all formations of vitality and all formations of life,
and entered the realm of nirvana without remainder.
First, through the power of his prior vows, fire arose and consumed his body;
then, from the midst of the void, the remains of his bones rained down.
At that time, the great assembly sighed with sorrow and marveled at this rare occurrence.
They vied with one another to collect the remains and erect a stūpa,
constantly making offerings of various fragrant flowers, precious banners, canopies, music, and lamps.
This record of the duration of the Dharma has been passed down through successive generations by the masters of antiquity, who have recited and upheld it without forgetting.
In order to cause all kings, ministers, elders, householders, and various patrons to thoroughly understand cause and effect,
and to cultivate weariness toward this body— which is like a plantain tree, an illusion, a mirage, or foam— subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
By cultivating various supreme deeds, they shall encounter and serve Maitreya in future lives;
through liberation from afflictions and the attainment of great nirvana, they will give rise to love and joy,
thereby protecting, upholding, and establishing the Buddha’s true Dharma so that it does not perish for a long time.
The Record of the Dharma-Abiding Spoken by the Great Arhat Nandimitra.
